headline: Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic adopt new scraping controls for AI training
summary: Major AI companies are committing to a new robots.txt directive, allowing publishers to prevent their content from being scraped for generative AI training.
details: Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft have committed to honoring a new robots.txt directive. This will allow publishers to specify their preferences regarding the scraping of their content for generative AI training.

The companies have decided to adopt a proposal under consideration at IETF, the open standards organization for the internet. This proposal was written by Anthropic technical lead for standards, Kevin Kelley.

Currently, website owners must identify individual crawlers and add separate rules for each provider. Kelley's proposal will change this by getting multiple AI companies to recognize and honor a single common signal.

Publishers will set up a new user agent in their robots.txt file specifically for AI training, which will look like "User-Agent: __usage_ai-training". This will block crawlers specifically meant to gather data for AI training.

The "Allow" section gives website operators the option to permit scraping for AI training for specific parts of a page, such as a press kit. This new user-agent section does not prevent crawling altogether or stop content from showing up on Google search.

Google will specifically interpret this directive as a stop sign for its "Google-Extended" user agent, which crawls websites for materials used to train Gemini models. It's important to note that this directive cannot undo any past scraping the companies have already done.
Anthropic has already started supporting the new directive. OpenAI pledged to implement the new signal in the coming months, while Microsoft and Google said they will support it in early 2027.

headline_marked: [[Meta's Muse AI agent has 'insignificant' business impact]] despite millions of users
headline: Meta's Muse AI agent has 'insignificant' business impact despite millions of users
summary: Meta claims millions use its Muse AI agent for shopping, with average purchases over $200. Yet, executives from 50 companies across various sectors report 'insignificant' activity, challenging fears of immediate market disruption.
details: Meta's Muse, an agentic AI tool designed to automate online tasks, has been a hot topic on corporate earnings calls. Meta claims millions of users are leveraging Muse for shopping, with average purchases exceeding $200.

Wall Street initially feared that proactive shopping assistants like Muse would erode brand loyalty, ignite price wars, and squeeze corporate profits. However, executives from roughly 50 companies across diverse sectors, including travel, food, and finance, have largely dismissed immediate disruption.

Food delivery app DoorDash reported only "hundreds" of orders from Muse and other agents. T-Mobile stated they've seen "nothing of significance," while Hilton called bookings from agents "insignificant."

Banking provider Ally Financial characterized agent activity as "quite low," and eBay termed it "very, very small." Fitness chain Life Time Group, Public Storage, and Hartford Insurance Group all reported "zero" cancellations or similar minimal data from agents.

Despite these reports, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg stated that over 10 million people in the US and Canada had activated Muse. He added that over 25 percent used it for shopping, exceeding the company's expectations.

Meta declined further comment but highlighted partnerships with 10 retailers, including Walmart, Best Buy, and Gap, to simplify shopping with Muse. Many of these partners reported earnings before Muse's launch and have not yet shared specific data.

Companies are acknowledging agents are in early stages but are already optimizing their websites. Chipotle, for instance, found agents struggled with loyalty discounts and after-hours ordering, leading to a single-digit percentage increase in agentic orders.

Chipotle is now tidying its website code to improve agent navigation, while DoorDash, Costco, and Extra Space Storage are also making similar optimizations. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, a Meta board member, even called the current hype around agents "delusional."

The reliance on agents could be costly, as Zuckerberg plans to charge businesses a fee for Muse-facilitated transactions, predicting this revenue will eventually surpass advertising. InterContinental Hotels CEO Elie Maalouf is taking a cautious approach in ongoing talks with Meta.

Security issues and errant orders remain a concern, with Bank of America warning customers about sharing login information with AI assistants. While some fear agents could encourage comparison shopping and hurt profits, executives suggest product quality, customer service, and brand trust will still be key factors.

Stances on agents are evolving quickly; Amazon initially blocked Muse in favor of its own Alexa shopping agent. However, the retail giant has since acknowledged that it anticipates working with outside agents in the future.
